results.title: How to prevent the “double counting” of emission reductions in the Paris Agreement | SEI
results.content: # How to prevent the “double counting” of emission reductions in the Paris Agreement. Countries must agree to a Paris Agreement rulebook that avoids the “double counting” of emission reductions, or risk undermining the agreement, according to a new study in *Science*. The study’s authors – including former SEI Associate Lambert Schneider, who is now Research Coordinator for International Climate Policy with the Institute for Applied Ecology (Oeko Institut), and SEI Senior Scientists Derik Broekhoff﻿﻿ and Michael Lazarus﻿﻿ – emphasize the need for common international accounting rules that protect against double-counting, or the use of the same emission reduction more than once to achieve climate mitigation targets. “To build a solid basis for international cooperation that can cost-effectively combat climate change, the Paris Agreement needs international carbon market rules that ensure environmental integrity and avoid double counting,” the authors wrote in the study.

results.title: Facebook Tightens Rules on Reposted Content - Tech Pacific
results.content: # Facebook Tightens Rules on Reposted Content. Facebook is increasing its efforts to limit accounts that repeatedly share other people's content without adding original input or value. | Facebook Tightens Rules on Reposted Content |. Facebook is now actively limiting the reach of duplicate content to ensure original creators receive the audience and engagement they deserve. Users who habitually share others' content without permission or original input may face temporary suspension from Facebook’s monetization tools. Meta is currently testing tools that attribute original content by including links back to the source when duplicates are identified. Content that includes third-party watermarks or clearly comes from another platform (e.g., TikTok) is likely to be flagged quickly. Content that encourages comments, shares, and meaningful discussion is more likely to be promoted—another reason to focus on original, engaging material rather than recycled posts. If you’re a creator and find your content being reused without credit, Facebook allows you to report the violation.

Title: Meta announces new rules to combat reposted content
* The Daily Dot X (formerly Twitter). # “Facebook aims to be a place where original content thrives”: Meta announces new rules to combat reposted content. One of the worst things about Facebook, Instagram, and really any Meta platform right now is its relentless stream of reposted content. However, on Facebook, at least, it appears that things are set to change. "Too often the same meme or video pops up repeatedly — sometimes from accounts pretending to be the creator and other times from different spammy accounts," YouTube said in a blog post."It dulls the experience for all and makes it harder for fresh voices to break through.". The platform then announces that creators who frequently repost content will be punished by losing access to Facebook's monetization programs. In addition to this, creators will see that their posts are getting less distribution. It works like this: when Facebook detects reposted content, it will reduce the distribution of these videos so the original clip doesn't lose out. The platform also reported that it's testing adding links to duplicate videos to pivot attention back to the original creator. This move is part of Meta's "long-term initiative" to crack down on what it describes as "spammy content." In just six months, Meta says it has taken action against 500 accounts that "engaged in spammy behavior or fake engagement." This involved demoting comments and reducing this content's distribution in order to prevent these accounts from monetizing. "Facebook aims to be a place where original content thrives, and creators are rewarded for their hard work and creativity," the platform concludes. "Stay tuned for more updates on our efforts to support creators like you.". ***The internet is chaotic—but we’ll break it down for you in one daily email.
